nodes.title: Part 1: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Part 1. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: A team migrating from raw Parquet files in S3 to Databricks Delta Lake wants to eliminate the partial-write and lost-update issues they used to see when multiple jobs wrote to the same dataset. Which Delta Lake characteristic addresses this?
flashcards.back: Delta Lake's `_delta_log/` directory — JSON action files plus periodic checkpoints — provides atomic, isolated, durable commits on cloud object storage through optimistic concurrency control. Concurrent writers each propose a commit and the log resolves conflicts, so there is no single-writer constraint. Snappy is compression, not concurrency. Row-level locks are not part of the Delta architecture; concurrency is handled per-file at commit time.

flashcards.front: An engineer is choosing the cluster type for a nightly transformation pipeline that runs from a scheduled Databricks Workflow. Cost efficiency is the priority. Which option is most appropriate?
flashcards.back: Job clusters (Jobs Compute) are created when the workflow starts and shut down as soon as the run finishes, so the team pays only for the actual run time and benefits from a lower DBU rate. All-purpose clusters are designed for interactive notebooks and carry a higher DBU rate. A 24/7 single-node cluster bills continuously even when idle. SQL warehouses are sized for BI / SQL workloads, not arbitrary Python or Scala job runs.

flashcards.front: An ingestion pipeline must continuously load many small JSON files dropped into an S3 prefix. The team needs schema evolution, exactly-once semantics, and low operational overhead as the file count grows into the millions. Which approach is recommended?
flashcards.back: Auto Loader's `cloudFiles` source incrementally discovers new files via a RocksDB-backed checkpoint (optionally enriched with cloud-provider file-notification events), scales to billions of files, and supports `cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode`. It is Databricks' recommended pattern for continuous file ingestion. `COPY INTO` is idempotent but is geared toward batch loads of a known file set. Vanilla Structured Streaming over a path re-lists the directory each batch and breaks down at high file counts. Nightly `dbutils.fs.ls` loops are neither exactly-once nor scalable.

flashcards.front: Inside a Delta Live Tables pipeline written in SQL, a developer must declare a table that incrementally consumes new rows appended to its upstream source on every pipeline update. Which DLT SQL form expresses this?
flashcards.back: A `STREAMING LIVE TABLE` in DLT processes input incrementally — each pipeline update sees only the rows appended to the source since the previous run, and Databricks manages the checkpoint for you. A plain `LIVE TABLE` (now `MATERIALIZED VIEW`) is fully recomputed on each refresh. `INCREMENTAL = TRUE` is not a DLT keyword.

questions.q: A team migrating from raw Parquet files in S3 to Databricks Delta Lake wants to eliminate the partial-write and lost-update issues they used to see when multiple jobs wrote to the same dataset. Which Delta Lake characteristic addresses this?
choices: A transaction log (`_delta_log/`) tracks each commit, providing ACID guarantees on top of object storage via optimistic concurrency control.
Delta tables disallow concurrent writers and require a single dedicated cluster per table.
Delta tables compress files with Snappy, which serialises writes by definition.
Delta tables require all writers to first acquire a row-level lock from the workspace metastore.
questions.explanation: Delta Lake's `_delta_log/` directory — JSON action files plus periodic checkpoints — provides atomic, isolated, durable commits on cloud object storage through optimistic concurrency control. Concurrent writers each propose a commit and the log resolves conflicts, so there is no single-writer constraint. Snappy is compression, not concurrency. Row-level locks are not part of the Delta architecture; concurrency is handled per-file at commit time.

questions.q: An engineer is choosing the cluster type for a nightly transformation pipeline that runs from a scheduled Databricks Workflow. Cost efficiency is the priority. Which option is most appropriate?
choices: An all-purpose cluster shared with analysts so the pipeline reuses warm executors.
A job cluster (Jobs Compute) that the workflow creates at the start of the run and terminates on completion.
A single-node cluster left running 24/7 in shared mode.
A Databricks SQL warehouse with auto-stop disabled.
questions.explanation: Job clusters (Jobs Compute) are created when the workflow starts and shut down as soon as the run finishes, so the team pays only for the actual run time and benefits from a lower DBU rate. All-purpose clusters are designed for interactive notebooks and carry a higher DBU rate. A 24/7 single-node cluster bills continuously even when idle. SQL warehouses are sized for BI / SQL workloads, not arbitrary Python or Scala job runs.

questions.q: An ingestion pipeline must continuously load many small JSON files dropped into an S3 prefix. The team needs schema evolution, exactly-once semantics, and low operational overhead as the file count grows into the millions. Which approach is recommended?
choices: A `COPY INTO` statement executed once per day from a scheduled job.
A plain Structured Streaming job that points at the raw S3 prefix and lists the directory each microbatch.
Auto Loader (`cloudFiles` source) inside a Structured Streaming query, with schema inference and evolution enabled.
A nightly notebook that calls `dbutils.fs.ls` and unions the results into a Parquet write.
questions.explanation: Auto Loader's `cloudFiles` source incrementally discovers new files via a RocksDB-backed checkpoint (optionally enriched with cloud-provider file-notification events), scales to billions of files, and supports `cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode`. It is Databricks' recommended pattern for continuous file ingestion. `COPY INTO` is idempotent but is geared toward batch loads of a known file set. Vanilla Structured Streaming over a path re-lists the directory each batch and breaks down at high file counts. Nightly `dbutils.fs.ls` loops are neither exactly-once nor scalable.

questions.q: Inside a Delta Live Tables pipeline written in SQL, a developer must declare a table that incrementally consumes new rows appended to its upstream source on every pipeline update. Which DLT SQL form expresses this?
choices: `CREATE LIVE TABLE sales AS SELECT * FROM source`
`CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW sales AS SELECT * FROM source`
`CREATE TABLE sales WITH (INCREMENTAL = TRUE) AS SELECT * FROM source`
`CREATE STREAMING LIVE TABLE sales AS SELECT * FROM STREAM(source)`
questions.explanation: A `STREAMING LIVE TABLE` in DLT processes input incrementally — each pipeline update sees only the rows appended to the source since the previous run, and Databricks manages the checkpoint for you. A plain `LIVE TABLE` (now `MATERIALIZED VIEW`) is fully recomputed on each refresh. `INCREMENTAL = TRUE` is not a DLT keyword.

questions.q: A nightly job accidentally overwrote the `sales` Delta table at 03:00 UTC with bad data. The team needs to read the contents of the table as they were just before the overwrite, without modifying the live table. Which query does that?
choices: `SELECT * FROM sales BEFORE TIMESTAMP '2026-01-15T03:00:00'`
`SELECT * FROM sales TIMESTAMP AS OF '2026-01-15T02:59:00'`
`SELECT * FROM sales SNAPSHOT '02:59:00'`
`SELECT * FROM sales ROLLBACK TO TIMESTAMP '2026-01-15T02:59:00'`
questions.explanation: Delta Time Travel exposes `TIMESTAMP AS OF <ts>` and `VERSION AS OF <n>` for read-only point-in-time queries against any historical snapshot the retention window still covers. `BEFORE TIMESTAMP`, `SNAPSHOT`, and `ROLLBACK TO` are not Delta syntax — `RESTORE TABLE … TO TIMESTAMP …` would actually mutate the table back to that version, which the prompt explicitly rules out.

questions.q: A team is creating tables in a Unity-Catalog-enabled workspace. How many object levels make up a fully qualified table name in Unity Catalog?
choices: Three: `catalog.schema.table` (with `schema` sometimes still called `database`).
Two: `database.table`, the same layout as the legacy Hive metastore.
Four: `metastore.catalog.schema.table`, where the metastore name is part of every identifier.
One: just `table`; both catalog and schema are inferred from the current cluster context.
questions.explanation: Unity Catalog introduced a three-level namespace — `catalog.schema.table`. The metastore is the top-level container but is not referenced inside a table identifier; you set it once per workspace. Legacy Hive metastores used a two-level `database.table` layout. Catalog and schema can be defaulted with `USE CATALOG` / `USE SCHEMA`, but the canonical identifier is still three parts.

questions.q: Business analysts query Delta tables from Power BI dashboards backed by Databricks SQL. The team wants compute that auto-scales between 2 and 8 clusters based on query concurrency, ships a JDBC/ODBC endpoint for the BI tool, and runs Photon by default. Which compute should they provision?
choices: An all-purpose cluster pool sized 2–8 with Photon enabled.
A Jobs Compute (job cluster) scheduled once per dashboard refresh.
A single-node cluster pinned to Photon mode.
A Pro SQL warehouse configured with auto-stop and a 2–8 cluster scaling range.
questions.explanation: Databricks SQL warehouses (Classic / Pro / Serverless) are the compute type designed for SQL analytics and BI dashboards. They expose a min/max cluster setting that auto-scales for query concurrency, ship a managed JDBC/ODBC endpoint, and enable Photon by default. All-purpose clusters auto-scale executors within a single cluster, not across multiple clusters. A job cluster is sized per run, not per dashboard query load.

questions.q: An engineer wants a full, independent point-in-time copy of a Delta table at a new location — data files plus history — so future deletes on the source cannot affect the copy. Which command fits best?
choices: `CREATE TABLE clone AS SELECT * FROM source` (CTAS)
`CREATE TABLE clone SHALLOW CLONE source`
`CREATE TABLE clone DEEP CLONE source`
`CONVERT TO DELTA source`
questions.explanation: `DEEP CLONE` copies both the data files and the transaction log to the target location, so the clone owns its own files and is unaffected by deletes or VACUUMs on the source. `SHALLOW CLONE` only copies metadata pointers — a delete on the source can break the clone. A CTAS query materialises the current snapshot but loses history (versions and time-travel queries). `CONVERT TO DELTA` upgrades existing Parquet to Delta in place; it does not produce a copy.

nodes.title: Part 2: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Part 2. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: After a large DELETE, an engineer runs `VACUUM sales RETAIN 0 HOURS` to immediately reclaim disk space. What is the principal risk of this command?
flashcards.back: VACUUM physically deletes files that are no longer referenced by the current table version and that are older than the retention window. With `RETAIN 0 HOURS`, files become eligible for removal the instant they are unreferenced, which can break in-flight reads and any time-travel query that points at an older snapshot. Databricks deliberately gates retention below the default seven days behind `spark.databricks.delta.retentionDurationCheck.enabled=false` for this reason. VACUUM does not lock the table, does not truncate the transaction log, and works on both managed and external Delta tables.

flashcards.front: A daily upsert job must merge a CDC source into the `customers` Delta table: insert new rows, update changed rows, and delete tombstoned rows — all in a single atomic statement. Which construct is designed for this?
flashcards.back: `MERGE INTO` is Delta's atomic upsert/delete primitive. It pairs a single source against a target and lets you specify any combination of `WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE`, `WHEN MATCHED THEN DELETE`, and `WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT` clauses, all committed in one transaction. `REPLACE WHERE` rewrites a partition wholesale; `INSERT OVERWRITE` replaces rows in bulk; there is no `UPDATE … FROM … UNION DELETE` form in Spark SQL.

flashcards.front: A multi-step Databricks Workflow needs Task B to run only after Task A succeeds, and Task C to run only after Task B succeeds. What is the right way to model this?
flashcards.back: Databricks Workflows expose a task DAG: each task has a `Depends on` list, and Databricks runs a task only when all of its parents have succeeded. This is the documented way to model ordering and is what shows up correctly in the run history, retries, and lineage. `dbutils.notebook.run` chains work imperatively but bypasses the workflow UI. Time-based cron coordination is fragile because a slow upstream run silently breaks the ordering.

flashcards.front: A data engineer must let the `bi_team` group read every current and future table in the `gold` schema of the `analytics` Unity catalog — and nothing else. Which set of grants is the least-privilege option that satisfies the requirement?
flashcards.back: Unity Catalog requires traversal privileges in addition to data privileges. `USE CATALOG` on the catalog and `USE SCHEMA` on the schema let the group reach the namespace; `SELECT ON SCHEMA` is inherited by every current and future table inside that schema, satisfying the future-proof requirement. `GRANT SELECT ON CATALOG analytics` would also work but exceeds the requested scope — it covers every schema under `analytics`, not just `gold`. `ALL PRIVILEGES` includes write rights. `USAGE` and `DATABASE` are legacy Hive metastore syntax that Unity Catalog does not use.

questions.q: After a large DELETE, an engineer runs `VACUUM sales RETAIN 0 HOURS` to immediately reclaim disk space. What is the principal risk of this command?
choices: Concurrent readers — including time-travel queries — referencing files older than the retention threshold will fail, because those files are physically removed.
VACUUM acquires a table-level lock for hours, blocking all writes and reads until it finishes.
VACUUM irreversibly truncates the transaction log, so the table can no longer be queried.
VACUUM only runs against managed tables; on an external table it silently no-ops.
questions.explanation: VACUUM physically deletes files that are no longer referenced by the current table version and that are older than the retention window. With `RETAIN 0 HOURS`, files become eligible for removal the instant they are unreferenced, which can break in-flight reads and any time-travel query that points at an older snapshot. Databricks deliberately gates retention below the default seven days behind `spark.databricks.delta.retentionDurationCheck.enabled=false` for this reason. VACUUM does not lock the table, does not truncate the transaction log, and works on both managed and external Delta tables.

questions.q: A daily upsert job must merge a CDC source into the `customers` Delta table: insert new rows, update changed rows, and delete tombstoned rows — all in a single atomic statement. Which construct is designed for this?
choices: `INSERT OVERWRITE customers SELECT … WHEN NOT EXISTS`
`UPDATE customers FROM cdc UNION DELETE FROM customers …`
`MERGE INTO customers USING cdc ON … WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE … WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT … WHEN MATCHED AND cdc.op='D' THEN DELETE`
`REPLACE WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT … FROM cdc)`
questions.explanation: `MERGE INTO` is Delta's atomic upsert/delete primitive. It pairs a single source against a target and lets you specify any combination of `WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE`, `WHEN MATCHED THEN DELETE`, and `WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT` clauses, all committed in one transaction. `REPLACE WHERE` rewrites a partition wholesale; `INSERT OVERWRITE` replaces rows in bulk; there is no `UPDATE … FROM … UNION DELETE` form in Spark SQL.

questions.q: A multi-step Databricks Workflow needs Task B to run only after Task A succeeds, and Task C to run only after Task B succeeds. What is the right way to model this?
choices: Replace Task B and Task C with `dbutils.notebook.run` calls invoked from inside Task A.
In the Workflow's task graph, add Task A as a dependency of Task B, and Task B as a dependency of Task C.
Schedule three separate jobs five minutes apart on cron so they fire in order.
Combine all three notebooks into one, gating each step with a `try/except` block.
questions.explanation: Databricks Workflows expose a task DAG: each task has a `Depends on` list, and Databricks runs a task only when all of its parents have succeeded. This is the documented way to model ordering and is what shows up correctly in the run history, retries, and lineage. `dbutils.notebook.run` chains work imperatively but bypasses the workflow UI. Time-based cron coordination is fragile because a slow upstream run silently breaks the ordering.

questions.q: A data engineer must let the `bi_team` group read every current and future table in the `gold` schema of the `analytics` Unity catalog — and nothing else. Which set of grants is the least-privilege option that satisfies the requirement?
choices: `GRANT SELECT ON CATALOG analytics TO `bi_team``
`GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON SCHEMA analytics.gold TO `bi_team``
`GRANT USAGE ON DATABASE gold TO `bi_team``
`GRANT USE CATALOG ON CATALOG analytics TO `bi_team``, `GRANT USE SCHEMA ON SCHEMA analytics.gold TO `bi_team``, and `GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA analytics.gold TO `bi_team``
questions.explanation: Unity Catalog requires traversal privileges in addition to data privileges. `USE CATALOG` on the catalog and `USE SCHEMA` on the schema let the group reach the namespace; `SELECT ON SCHEMA` is inherited by every current and future table inside that schema, satisfying the future-proof requirement. `GRANT SELECT ON CATALOG analytics` would also work but exceeds the requested scope — it covers every schema under `analytics`, not just `gold`. `ALL PRIVILEGES` includes write rights. `USAGE` and `DATABASE` are legacy Hive metastore syntax that Unity Catalog does not use.

questions.q: A Delta table receives a daily CDC feed with inserts, updates, and deletes keyed by `id`. The team needs an idempotent upsert-and-delete in one statement. Which approach is correct?
choices: Use a single `MERGE INTO` with `WHEN MATCHED ... UPDATE`, `WHEN MATCHED ... DELETE`, and `WHEN NOT MATCHED ... INSERT` clauses.
Run separate `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE` statements in a transaction block.
`OVERWRITE` the whole table each day with the CDC batch.
Append the CDC rows and rely on `VACUUM` to remove the superseded versions.
questions.explanation: `MERGE INTO` applies inserts, updates, and deletes in a single atomic statement matched on a key, which is exactly the pattern for applying a CDC batch idempotently. You can include multiple `WHEN MATCHED` clauses (one to UPDATE, one to DELETE on a flag) plus a `WHEN NOT MATCHED` INSERT. Databricks SQL does not expose multi-statement BEGIN/COMMIT transaction blocks across separate DML the way this option implies; overwriting the entire table daily is wasteful and loses history; and `VACUUM` only removes old files past the retention window — it does not apply updates or deletes to logical rows.

questions.q: A Delta Live Tables pipeline defines a table with an expectation `CONSTRAINT valid_id EXPECT (id IS NOT NULL) ON VIOLATION DROP ROW`. What happens to rows where `id` is null?
choices: The pipeline fails immediately on the first null id.
Rows with a null id are dropped from the target and the violation is recorded in the pipeline's data-quality metrics.
Rows with a null id are written anyway but flagged with a hidden column.
The null ids are automatically replaced with a generated surrogate key.
questions.explanation: In DLT, `EXPECT ... ON VIOLATION DROP ROW` removes records that fail the constraint from the target table while allowing the pipeline to continue, and the number of dropped rows is captured in the pipeline's data-quality event log/metrics. `ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE` (not this clause) is what stops the pipeline; a bare `EXPECT` keeps violating rows but reports them. DLT does not silently write violating rows with a hidden flag under DROP ROW, nor does it fabricate surrogate keys for nulls.

questions.q: After many small MERGE operations, a Delta table has thousands of tiny files and queries have slowed. Which maintenance command consolidates small files, and what does it NOT do by itself?
choices: `VACUUM` compacts small files; it does not remove old versions.
`REFRESH TABLE` compacts small files; it does not update statistics.
`OPTIMIZE` compacts small files into larger ones; it does not physically delete old file versions (that is `VACUUM`'s job).
`ANALYZE TABLE` compacts small files; it does not change the layout.
questions.explanation: `OPTIMIZE` performs bin-packing compaction, rewriting many small files into fewer large ones to speed reads (and with `ZORDER BY`, co-locates data by columns). It does not reclaim storage from now-unreferenced old files — that requires `VACUUM`, which deletes files older than the retention threshold. `VACUUM` removes versions but does not compact for performance, `REFRESH TABLE` only invalidates cached metadata, and `ANALYZE TABLE` collects statistics rather than rewriting file layout.

questions.q: A job must run three notebooks where task B and task C both depend on task A, and B and C can run in parallel. What is the correct way to express this in Databricks Workflows?
choices: Put all three notebooks in one task and call them with `%run`, which parallelizes automatically.
Use a single-task job and rely on Spark to schedule the notebooks as stages.
Create three separate jobs and trigger them with cron times spaced one minute apart.
Create a multi-task job with three tasks and set B and C to each depend on A, so B and C run in parallel after A succeeds.
questions.explanation: Databricks Workflows model dependencies as a DAG of tasks: create one job with three tasks and set the 'depends on' of both B and C to A. Once A succeeds, B and C start and run concurrently, which is exactly the required topology. `%run` includes another notebook inline and runs sequentially in one context (no parallel DAG). Spacing separate cron jobs a minute apart is fragile and does not enforce the real dependency, and a single task cannot express inter-notebook dependencies.

nodes.title: Cloud governance: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Governance is the set of policies and guardrails that keep a cloud account safe and on-budget as it scales from one engineer to a hundred. Think tagging standards, budget alerts, organizational policies, and the multi-account strategy.

flashcards.front: Why use multiple accounts (an Organization) instead of one big account?
flashcards.back: Blast-radius isolation: a compromised prod account doesn't leak into dev. Billing clarity: per-team or per-environment cost reports. Quota independence: prod doesn't share API limits with sandbox. Service Control Policies (AWS) / management groups (Azure) enforce 'no one can disable CloudTrail' across the whole org.

flashcards.front: What is a Service Control Policy (SCP)?
flashcards.back: An AWS Organizations policy that sets the maximum permissions any IAM identity in a member account can have. Even if a user's IAM policy grants `s3:*`, an SCP denying `s3:DeleteBucket` overrides it. SCPs are guardrails, not grants — they only restrict.

flashcards.front: Tagging strategy — name three high-leverage tags.
flashcards.back: (1) Owner / team — who pays and who to page. (2) Environment (prod/staging/dev) — drives access controls and lifecycle. (3) Cost-center / project — for chargeback. Tags are free and infinitely valuable for cost allocation and automation; enforce them with policies.

A pre-baked multi-account setup with security baselines: org with master + audit + log-archive + workload accounts, CloudTrail / Config enabled everywhere, SSO wired up, network templates ready. AWS Control Tower / Azure Landing Zones / GCP setup automate this so you start on a safe foundation, not bare cloud.

questions.q: A team needs an interactive cluster for exploratory notebook work by several analysts during the day, and a separate compute for a scheduled nightly ETL job. Which choice minimizes cost while fitting each use?
choices: Use an all-purpose cluster (with autoscaling and auto-termination) for interactive work, and a job cluster that spins up per run for the scheduled ETL.
Use one always-on all-purpose cluster for both, to avoid startup latency.
Use a SQL warehouse for the ETL job and an all-purpose cluster for the interactive work and the ETL.
Use a single-node cluster for the ETL and share it with the analysts.
questions.explanation: All-purpose (interactive) clusters are designed for collaborative notebook work and should use autoscaling plus auto-termination to avoid paying for idle time. Scheduled jobs should run on job (automated) clusters that are created for the run and terminated at the end — this is billed at the cheaper Jobs Compute rate and avoids a persistent cluster. Keeping one always-on cluster wastes money overnight, forcing all ETL onto an interactive cluster mixes workloads and costs more, and sharing a single-node cluster between a heavy ETL and several analysts creates contention.

questions.q: A downstream report accidentally read a Delta table after a bad batch overwrote it. The team must recover the table state from before the bad write, which happened 3 versions ago. Which capability and command apply?
choices: Structured Streaming checkpoints: replay the stream from offset 0.
Delta time travel: read or roll back with `VERSION AS OF` or `RESTORE TABLE ... TO VERSION AS OF`, within the retention window.
Unity Catalog lineage: click 'undo' on the table.
`REFRESH TABLE`: it reloads the pre-write cached copy.
questions.explanation: Delta Lake retains a versioned transaction log, so you can query a past state with `SELECT ... VERSION AS OF n` (or `TIMESTAMP AS OF`) and roll the table back with `RESTORE TABLE ... TO VERSION AS OF n` — as long as the underlying files have not been removed by `VACUUM` beyond the retention window. Streaming checkpoints track stream progress, not table snapshots; Unity Catalog lineage visualizes relationships but offers no 'undo' button; and `REFRESH TABLE` only invalidates cached metadata, it does not restore old data.

questions.q: In Unity Catalog, an analyst can query a table through a SQL warehouse but gets 'permission denied' running the same query from an all-purpose cluster. The grants on the table are identical. What is the most likely cause?
choices: SQL warehouses ignore Unity Catalog permissions entirely.
Table grants only apply to the workspace admin.
The all-purpose cluster is not in a Unity-Catalog-compatible access mode (shared or single-user with UC enabled), so it cannot resolve the grants.
The table must be re-created as external for cluster access.
questions.explanation: Unity Catalog governance is only enforced on clusters running a UC-compatible access mode (shared, or single-user assigned to the user, with UC enabled). A cluster in a legacy/no-isolation mode cannot resolve UC grants, so the same query that works on a SQL warehouse (always UC-aware) fails there. SQL warehouses do honor UC permissions, table grants apply to any granted principal (not just admins), and the managed-vs-external distinction is about storage/lifecycle, not whether a cluster can read it.

questions.q: A streaming query reads from a Delta table and writes to another with a checkpoint location configured. The job is stopped and restarted after a code change. What is the role of the checkpoint on restart?
choices: It reprocesses the entire source from the beginning to guarantee correctness.
It is optional metadata and has no effect on restart behavior.
It caches the output data so restarts are faster.
It stores the stream's progress (offsets) and state so the query resumes from where it left off, providing exactly-once processing.
questions.explanation: A Structured Streaming checkpoint persists the source offsets and any operator state, so on restart the query resumes from the last committed progress rather than reprocessing everything — this is what enables end-to-end exactly-once semantics with Delta sinks. It is not a data cache for speed, and it is far from optional: without a stable checkpoint location the stream cannot track what it has consumed and would risk reprocessing or data loss.

questions.q: A team wants a lightweight, metadata-only copy of a large Delta table for a short-lived experiment, without duplicating the underlying data files. Which clone type fits, and what is its main caveat?
choices: SHALLOW CLONE, which copies only metadata and references the source's data files (breaks if those files are VACUUMed away).
DEEP CLONE, because it never copies data.
CREATE TABLE AS SELECT, which is the only way to clone.
A view, because a view physically copies the data for isolation.
questions.explanation: A SHALLOW CLONE creates a new table that copies the source metadata and points at the source's existing data files, making it fast and storage-cheap for short-lived experiments. Its caveat is exactly that dependence: if the source files are removed by `VACUUM`, the shallow clone's references become invalid. DEEP CLONE is the one that copies the data files (durable but heavier), CTAS materializes a full independent copy, and a view stores no data at all — it is just a saved query.

questions.q: A raw JSON source has an evolving schema — new fields appear over time. An Auto Loader stream into a bronze Delta table must not fail when new columns arrive, and should capture them. Which configuration achieves this?
choices: Disable schema inference and hard-code the schema so new fields are ignored silently.
Enable Auto Loader schema inference with schema evolution (`cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode` addNewColumns) and a schema location so new columns are added to the table.
Set the stream to `OVERWRITE` mode so each batch redefines the schema.
Use `mergeSchema=false` on the write to force new columns into a single string column.
questions.explanation: Auto Loader supports schema evolution: with a configured schema location and evolution mode `addNewColumns`, when a new field appears the stream updates the schema and adds the column (the stream restarts to pick up the change) rather than failing. Hard-coding the schema silently drops new data, `OVERWRITE` mode is not how a bronze append-ingest stream should behave and does not solve evolution, and `mergeSchema=false` prevents new columns from being added at all — the opposite of the requirement.

finalBoss.title: Final Exam: Databricks Certified Data Engineer Associate
